title: Population pyramids

blocks.heading: Population pyramids
blocks.text: A population pyramid shows age and sex composition, with age groups vertically and horizontal bars for each sex on a consistent count or percentage scale. A broad base indicates a relatively large young group; a narrower base and substantial older groups suggest a different age structure. Shape alone does not prove causes or future certainty.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Older age structures
blocks.text:
Many developed economies have relatively narrower young bases and larger older shares than youthful populations. These tendencies can inform care and workforce questions but do not describe every country or person. Compare the same age bands and units.

Applied example: A larger older-age share can increase demand for pensions and accessible care. A smaller working-age share can face greater support responsibilities relative to its size.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Youthful age structures
blocks.text:
A youthful pyramid has a relatively broad young base compared with older age groups. A large school-age share can imply future education demand, while future births also depend on survival, migration and fertility choices; do not infer inevitable rapid growth from shape alone.

Applied example: Many children increase present demand for schools and child services. As those cohorts reach working age, more employment and further training opportunities may be needed.

blocks.heading: Apply the measure
blocks.text: Describe the population-pyramid pattern represented by this original age-sex table: A, 0–14 male 20% female 20%, 15–64 male 27% female 27%, 65+ male 3% female 3%; B, 0–14 male 10% female 10%, 15–64 male 30% female 30%, 65+ male 10% female 10%. A has the broader young base, 40% versus 20%, while B has the larger older share, 20% versus 6%. The age structures suggest different education and care demands, without proving causes.

blocks.heading: Read and construct the shape
blocks.text: For the fictional table above, place age groups vertically, youngest at the bottom, and percentage bars horizontally, male left and female right. Use equal scales, a sex key, units and a title. A’s base bars extend 20% each side and older bars 3%; B’s are 10% and 10%. The age bands here are broad summaries; use finer equal bands for detailed age comparisons. No unseen plotted image is claimed to have been verified.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Explain a pyramid before planning services
blocks.text: A broad base indicates a large young share, commonly associated with relatively high recent births; it does not prove one cause. A youthful population can increase demand for schools, child services and later jobs. A higher older-age share can increase demand for accessible health care, pensions and support services, while a smaller working-age share may face greater support responsibilities. Numbers matter as well as percentages: the same age share in a larger population means more people. Check cohort size, migration and changing births or survival before using a pyramid to explain a trend.
